title: Lesson 38: Governor-Limit-Aware Design: SOQL, SOSL, and DML Budgets
description: The arithmetic behind limit exceptions: how SOQL statements, query rows, DML statements, and DML rows are metered, and why the statement and row meters fail at completely different batch sizes.

questions.question: A loop updates one record per iteration and fails at the 151st update. Which meter fired?
options: The DML row meter, which caps at 10,000 rows per transaction.
The query row meter, which caps at 50,000 returned rows.
The DML statement meter, at 150, while the row meter is barely used.
The SOQL statement meter, which caps at 100 queries per transaction.
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are independent meters, so per-record updates exhaust the 150-statement budget while the row meter has barely moved; batching into one call on a list fixes it.

questions.question: Moving a transaction to asynchronous execution raises which budgets?
options: All of them, including the DML row and SOQL row ceilings.
The query, heap, and CPU budgets, but not the DML or row limits.
Only the DML statement limit, which roughly doubles in async code.
None; asynchronous code is governed by the same limits as sync code.
questions.explanation: Async execution roughly doubles the query count and raises heap and CPU, but DML stays at 150 statements and 10,000 rows and SOQL rows stay at 50,000, so async alone will not save a DML-row failure.

questions.question: A save fires your trigger, a record-triggered flow, and an uncertified installed package. Whose budget do they spend?
options: Each of the three gets its own separate allocation.
Only the trigger and the flow share, because every package is isolated.
The package brings its own pool, because installed packages are certified.
One pool owned by the transaction, so headroom counts every consumer.
questions.explanation: Every process that fires on a save spends from one transaction budget, and only certified packages get their own pool, so a design review must leave headroom for automation you did not write.
